source.name: BBC Business
source.title: I earn £30,000. I'm angry there was no fuel duty cut in the Budget
source.summary: People on a range of incomes from £4,062 to £150,000 a year tell the BBC what they made of this year's Budget.
source.evidence_text:
BBC News has been speaking to people on a range of incomes on how they feel about their finances and how the Budget affects them.
Dave Herbert, a professional driver who moves cars between showrooms and does deliveries, says fuel prices have been "crazy" this year.
He spends around £350 a month on petrol for work and personal use. That's 40% to 50% more than at the start of the year, he says.
The only measure Dave wanted to see was a cut to fuel duty, and he was disappointed this didn't happen.
"I'm pretty angry, really. Nothing has been thrown my way," he says.
The 19-year-old from Swindon wants to be an animator but in the meantime is applying for retail and sales roles and apprenticeships. Most of the time, she doesn't hear back from potential employers.
She wants to see more funding to businesses so they can take on more young employees. She'd also like to see more money for training and the government's Jobs Guarantee , external scheme extended.
Robert Portlock, 29, has always lived with his parents in Gateshead and would love to move out. But he doesn't think he can afford to.
Rent would be his biggest concern, he says, explaining that a small flat in his area would cost him about two-thirds of his monthly wage.
She lives with her 16-year-old son, and says her energy bill has risen sharply over the past year and she now pays about £200 a month on gas and electricity.
Chloe, 40, and her son have cut back on luxuries like going to M&S and the cinema, and she now tries to limit the weekly food shop to £40.
Cutting standing charges on gas, and the £100 household energy payment for households in council tax bands A to D this winter are "definitely going to help", she says.
Emily Nelson completed her A-levels last year and like thousands of her peers has been unable to find a job since leaving college.
Chloe says she is "pretty happy" with the Budget, and that "small changes give me hope".
However, he wanted taxes to be put up for higher earners like himself in the name of "redistribution" and says there was "nothing" in the Budget on that.
"If we want better roads, hospitals, schools we need to raise more tax," he adds.
People on a range of incomes from £4,062 to £150,000 a year tell the BBC what they made of this year's Budget.
The 48-year-old, who is married with a 12-year-old daughter, says he has to find the extra money for fuel "from an already tight budget" and "dreads" filling up at the pump.
The main fuel duty rate has been frozen at 57.95p per litre since March 2011, and it will be frozen again, but Dave says: "It sounds like they're giving us something by keeping it frozen but they're actually still taking it off us."
Emily was initially disappointed with the Budget, and then frustrated that the government is waiting for the outcome of a review into youth unemployment before legislating next year.
The scheme, being rolled out across England, Scotland and Wales, guarantees fully funded, six-month paid jobs for 18 to 24-year-olds who have been on universal credit and looking for work for 18 months. But Emily thinks people should be eligible after a year.
Robert's biggest expense currently is his car, which he says he needs for his 32-mile round trip to work at Newcastle Airport. But he's paying £750 a month in car finance, insurance, fuel and tax.
She's very grateful that the rent she pays on her south London maisonette is set below the market rate as it is housing association accommodation, but says life was easier when she shared the bills. "Two incomes make a massive difference."
His daughters will start their working lives with between £45,000 to £60,000 of debt each, plus interest, which will be compounding at £5,000 to £8,000 per year.
"I have no objection to paying for degrees as I think they are a great way of broadening horizons and having great life experience. But I think the interest should be waived or capped below 1%, otherwise it's a noose around their neck for a substantial part of their lifetime."
"It is very difficult to balance the books," the 78-year-old says. "I do go on holiday, but I'm spending more of my savings to live."
The chancellor said standing charges would be removed from gas bills , but Christine, who has a gas boiler, says it's not clear yet whether she will benefit, because those costs will be added on to the unit rate.
However, she says the £100 household energy payment will help over the winter
"I'm not sure I'll be better off," she says. Instead she thinks she will be "even Stevens".

grammar.explanation: Use the present perfect for a situation that began in the past and continues now. Form it with “have” or “has” plus a past participle. In the reading, “has been unable” connects Emily's past difficulty with her situation now, while “since” introduces when that situation began.
grammar.example_quote: Emily Nelson has been unable to find a job since leaving college last year.

People judge the Budget differently because their financial needs differ.
Everyone believes higher taxes are the best solution.
option_feedback: Several people describe financial problems that remain.
Dave, Chloe and the higher earner judge the Budget according to different needs and priorities.
The higher earner supports higher taxes for people with large incomes, but the reading does not give this view to everyone.

lesson.title: Budget Divides Households Over Relief, Opportunity and Fairness
lesson.overview: Responses to the Budget reveal contrasting priorities, from immediate financial relief and access to employment to redistribution and uncertainty over actual savings.
lesson.topic: Household finances and responses to the Budget

vocabulary.definition: The capacity within a budget to meet additional costs without financial difficulty.
A minimum requirement someone must meet to qualify for support or an opportunity; here, a specified period of seeking work.
Use up part of someone's available income, leaving less for other expenses.
A price lower than the amount normally charged for comparable accommodation or services.
The use of taxation and public support to shift income or wealth between groups, especially towards those with less.
Accumulating as interest is added to a debt and further interest is calculated on the enlarged amount.
Formally not required to be paid, although the charge would otherwise apply.
Restricted by an upper limit, without necessarily being removed.
Keep income and expenditure in balance so that costs do not exceed available money.
Reduce or cancel the financial effect of a saving through a cost elsewhere.

grammar.explanation: In “While he accepts paying for university degrees, he argues that interest should be waived or capped below 1%.”, “while” means “although”, rather than indicating simultaneous events. The subordinate clause acknowledges his acceptance of degree costs before the main clause qualifies that position by challenging the associated interest.
grammar.example_quote: While he accepts paying for university degrees, he argues that interest should be waived or capped below 1%.

quiz.question: Which interpretation best captures the range of responses presented in the brief?
options: The interviewees assess the Budget chiefly through whether it reduces their tax rates.
The interviewees assess the Budget through different pressures, priorities and expectations of relief.
The interviewees agree that modest assistance has little practical or emotional value.
option_feedback: Employment access, housing costs and energy charges also shape the responses, so tax rates alone are too narrow a focus.
Dave prioritises fuel costs, Emily employment access, and another interviewee redistribution, while Christine questions the overall savings.
Chloe welcomes small changes, so this conclusion does not represent the range of views.

quiz.question: What does Dave's limited “financial headroom” imply in this context?
options: He has little capacity to absorb higher fuel costs within his existing budget.
He has reduced his fuel use enough to protect the rest of his budget.
He regards his fuel bill as substantial but readily manageable.
option_feedback: “Financial headroom” concerns the capacity to manage additional costs, which his strained budget offers little of.
The brief reports increased costs and financial pressure, without establishing a reduction in fuel use.
“Little financial headroom” indicates difficulty accommodating costs, rather than confidence in managing them.

quiz.question: Which reason supported by the brief explains why the fuel duty freeze fails to meet Dave's preference?
options: The freeze postpones the decision about whether the rate will rise.
The freeze lowers the rate without guaranteeing a lower overall fuel bill.
The freeze maintains the rate, whereas he wanted it reduced.
option_feedback: The brief presents the freeze as a decision to maintain the rate, rather than a postponed decision.
A freeze leaves the rate unchanged; it does not lower it.
Dave wanted a reduction, so maintaining the existing rate does not deliver the change he sought.

quiz.question: Which change would address Emily's stated concern about the employment scheme's “eligibility threshold”?
options: Retaining the waiting period while increasing the duration of the jobs.
Allowing applicants to qualify after a year of seeking work rather than 18 months.
Completing the unemployment review while leaving the waiting period unchanged.
option_feedback: Changing job duration would leave the waiting requirement she challenges intact.
Her proposed change concerns earlier eligibility, specifically reducing the period from 18 months to a year.
Completing the review would not itself introduce the shorter waiting period she favours.

quiz.question: Which inference about Robert's position is best supported?
options: He could resolve his housing difficulty simply by treating his car as optional.
He regards housing costs as manageable provided that rent remains his largest expense.
His prospects of independent housing are constrained by both potential rent and substantial transport costs.
option_feedback: He says he needs the car for his commute, so treating it as readily optional overlooks an explicit constraint.
Rent would be his biggest concern and would absorb about two-thirds of his monthly wage; this does not establish that he considers the burden manageable.
The brief places the prospective rent burden alongside significant car costs that he associates with getting to work.

quiz.question: What does Chloe's response contribute to the brief's overall account?
options: It shows that someone can welcome modest measures while still acknowledging financial pressures.
It establishes that lower housing costs remove the need for further household assistance.
It suggests that welcoming the Budget depends on expecting a major financial improvement.
option_feedback: She values small Budget changes while acknowledging that sharing bills previously made life easier.
She values her housing arrangement, but the brief does not present it as eliminating other financial pressures.
Her response explicitly values small changes, so a major improvement is not a stated condition of her support.

quiz.question: What distinguishes the higher earner's position on “redistribution” from a preference for reducing his own tax bill?
options: He wants higher earners to receive a larger share of the available relief.
He supports higher taxation for a group that explicitly includes himself.
He believes that university interest should replace taxation as a means of redistribution.
option_feedback: His stated preference is for higher earners to pay more tax, rather than receive more relief.
By including himself among those who should pay more, he supports redistribution despite its potential personal cost.
The brief presents university interest and redistribution as separate concerns; it does not propose replacing taxation with interest.

quiz.question: What mechanism does “compounding” identify in the account of the daughters' debts?
options: The debt being divided into equal annual repayments.
The interest rate being progressively reduced as the debt grows.
Interest being added to the debt and becoming part of the amount on which further interest is calculated.
option_feedback: “Compounding” describes how interest accumulates, rather than how repayments are divided.
“Compounding” does not imply a falling interest rate; it concerns the amount on which interest is calculated.
This captures the process explained in the vocabulary definition: accumulated interest can itself attract further interest.

quiz.question: What distinction matters in the proposal that interest should be “waived or capped below 1%”?
options: A waiver removes the requirement to pay the interest, whereas a cap limits the rate.
A waiver delays the interest charge, whereas a cap transfers it to another borrower.
A waiver limits the rate, whereas a cap cancels the original university debt.
option_feedback: “Waived” means the charge is not required to be paid; “capped” sets an upper limit while allowing a charge to remain.
Neither “waived” nor “capped” means postponing or transferring the charge in this context.
The meanings are misassigned, and limiting interest does not mean cancelling the original debt.

quiz.question: Which reason supported by the brief explains Christine's uncertainty about removing fixed gas charges?
options: She expects the winter energy allowance to be withdrawn if the charges disappear.
She believes the fixed charges will remain unchanged despite the announcement.
She understands that shifting costs into the unit rate could offset the apparent saving.
option_feedback: She expects the allowance to help; the brief does not link its availability to retaining fixed charges.
Her concern is about transferring costs into another part of the bill, rather than keeping the fixed charges unchanged.
Her uncertainty concerns the total bill: removing one charge may not yield a corresponding overall saving.

quiz.question: What is the effect of “While” in the sentence about accepting degree costs but questioning interest?
options: It explains that the objection to interest arises from opposition to university education.
It acknowledges acceptance of degree costs before introducing a qualification concerning interest.
It places acceptance and objection in two successive periods of the interviewee's life.
option_feedback: The subordinate clause establishes acceptance of degree costs, so it does not support opposition to university education.
The concessive structure allows acceptance of the general principle to coexist with criticism of an associated charge.
Here, “while” expresses concession, rather than a sequence of events.

quiz.question: Which sentence uses concessive “while” to express a contrast supported by Christine's account?
options: While Christine expects the winter allowance to help, she remains unsure whether she will be better off overall.
While Christine waits for winter, she considers how much her gas bill might change.
While Christine expects the winter allowance to help, she is certain that her overall finances will improve.
option_feedback: “While” means “although”, contrasting a specific expected benefit with uncertainty about the overall outcome.
This sentence is grammatical, but “while” has a temporal meaning here, and the brief does not describe this activity.
The concessive structure is grammatical, but the assertion of certainty contradicts Christine's reported uncertainty.
